```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "75%")
library(fixest)
library(modelsummary)
hh <- arrow::read_parquet("data/household_panel_w5.parquet")
```

# Question

Do households with a higher rent burden commute further, once we
control for income, household composition and region? The idea, from
@glaeser2008 and others, is that households trade housing costs
against commuting costs. The panel has `r nrow(hh)` household-waves
from `r dplyr::n_distinct(hh$hh_id)` households.

Rent burden is defined as monthly rent divided by net monthly
household income. A household paying $900 rent on an income of $3,000
has a burden of 0.30.

# Model

The baseline specification is

$$
\log(\text{dist}_{it}) = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \beta \, \text{burden}_{it}
  + \mathbf{x}_{it}'\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \varepsilon_{it}
$$

with household fixed effects $\alpha_i$ and wave fixed effects
$\lambda_t$. Standard errors are clustered by household. The
coefficient of interest is $\beta$; a positive value means that within
the same household, years with higher burden are years with longer
commutes.

```{r m1}
m1 <- feols(log(commute_km) ~ rent_burden + log(income) + n_children |
              hh_id + wave,
            data = hh, cluster = ~hh_id)
```

```{r m2}
m2 <- feols(log(commute_km) ~ rent_burden * urban + log(income) +
              n_children | hh_id + wave,
            data = hh, cluster = ~hh_id)
```

```{r tbl-models, echo=FALSE}
modelsummary(list("Baseline" = m1, "Urban interaction" = m2),
             stars = TRUE, gof_omit = "AIC|BIC|RMSE")
```

# Results so far

The baseline estimate is $\hat\beta =$ `r round(coef(m1)["rent_burden"], 3)`,
which would imply that a 10-point increase in burden is associated
with roughly a `r round(100 * (exp(0.1 * coef(m1)["rent_burden"]) - 1), 1)`%
longer commute. The interaction model suggests the relationship is
concentrated in urban areas, which makes sense: rural households have
fewer housing options within any given distance.

```{r fig-margins, fig.cap="Predicted log commute distance by rent burden, urban vs. rural.", echo=FALSE}
plot_predictions <- marginaleffects::plot_predictions
plot_predictions(m2, condition = c("rent_burden", "urban"))
```

## Caveats

1. Reverse causality is plausible: a new job further away could push
   a household to move somewhere cheaper. The fixed effects do not
   rule this out.
2. Commute distance is self-reported and heaped at round numbers
   (5, 10, 20 km).
3. The panel loses about 8% of households per wave, and attrition is
   higher among renters [@lynn2009, ch. 4].

# Things to try

- Re-estimate with commute *time* rather than distance.
- Check whether results change if we drop households that moved
  between waves.
